articles.title: The Debut review – Julianne Moore is a thrill in Jesse Eisenberg’s oddball comedy
articles.summary: Toronto film festival: riotous lead performance holds together third movie from actor turned film-maker, about a housewife who joins a local musical. Jesse Eisenberg’s last two directorial efforts – the prickly comedy When You Finish Saving the World and the slightly softer A Real Pain – are small…
body: The Debut is about a repressed housewife, Mona (Julianne Moore), who decides to audition for a role in a community theater production of a musical called Nosy Neighbors, one of those gassy Manhattan trifles that were so ubiquitous on Broadway a half century ago. Mona’s kids are about to fly the nest, and her husband barely seems to notice her when she’s standing right next to him. So why not have a little creative adventure?

From that setup, Eisenberg could have gone to the obvious place, staging a sweet dramedy about a humble act of artistic expression opening Mona’s eyes to all the possibility of life outside her little bubble. He does do that, in part, but he also wants to take things to a darker place. The film gradually morphs into a study of actorly obsession and vanity, as Mona takes the Stanislavksi-esque teachings of the play’s director, Jerry (Paul Giamatti, doing his wearily charming thing), to extremes perhaps not seen since Black Swan. That’s a clever idea: a director watching in horror as the monster he’s created threatens to lay waste to his production.

articles.title: Venice best actress winner says she signed on at Danish job centre days before her victory
articles.summary: Mathilde Arcel, who won the Volpi Cup on Saturday for her role in Golden Lion winner Woman Unknown, said job offers have now begun to arrive. The winner of this year’s best actress prize at the Venice film festival has revealed that she is on unemployment benefits and had to fly to back to…
body: On Saturday night, Danish actor Mathilde Arcel won the prestigious Volpi Cup for her first leading role in a feature film, May el-Toukhy’s post-second world war drama Woman Unknown, which also won the Golden Lion award for best film.
Jury president Maggie Gyllenhaal said the judges had been able to relax Venice rules around not awarding more than one prize per film because the vote for Arcel had been unanimous.

After her triumph, the 30-year-old actor revealed in interviews with Danish media that she had returned to Denmark after her film’s premiere to sign on at the job centre, as she is on unemployment benefits when not working on films. She then returned to the Lido after being told it would be wise to be present at the awards gala.
In the UK, actors’ trade union Equity said in a 2023 report that 63% of its members have been in receipt of social security at some point in their life.

articles.title: Sheryl Crow Serenaded by Olivia Rodrigo, Chris Stapleton, Jason Isbell and Other Stars at BMI Troubadour Tribute in Nashville
articles.summary: The lure of paying tribute to Sheryl Crow in speech and song brought out the big guns at an event honoring the singer-songwriter in Nashville Monday night, as Olivia Rodrigo, Chris Stapleton, Jason Isbell, Lauren Daigle, Eric Church and Melissa Etheridge all turned out to turn in stellar covers of…
body: Crow was receiving the BMI Troubadour Award, typically given to artists who fall into the realms of Americana and/or rootsy rock ‘n’ roll, with previous honorees ranging from John Fogerty to Lucinda Williams. As perhaps the biggest non-country music star living and working in Nashville, Crow was a shoo-in to be selected for that honor, with a guest list befitting her stature and a mini-tribute concert that won’t soon be forgotten by the couple hundred industry guests.

All of the guests sang backed by a house band of Music City stalwarts, Rodrigo was the biggest surprise of the night, having flown in to sing “Strong Enough” in Crow’s honor. Other performances included Isbell kicking off the evening’s performances with “Run Baby Run,” followed by Etheridge singing “If It Makes You Happy,” Daigle doing “Every Day Is a Winding Road,” Eric Church performing “Leaving Las Vegas” and Stapleton tearing into “I Shall Believe.”

articles.title: Ed Sheeran Says Dropping Macklemore From Tour Was ‘Promoter’s Decision, Not Mine,’ Explains Why He’s Not Speaking Out on Israel and Palestine
articles.summary: Ed Sheeran has commented on the decision to drop Macklemore from his U.S. Loop tour after the rapper made forceful “free Palestine” comments on stage during a political speech during the rapper’s performances opening for the singer at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey on Sept. 4 and 5.
body: “Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter’s decision, it was not mine. Macklemore’s contract for the tour was with the promoter, not me.
“I would never let down the fans who had made plans, nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living.

“I have always used my platform and music to bring people from all backgrounds and cultures together and this won’t ever change. Those who have been to one of my shows will know that they are about unity, joy, escapism, love, and a place for everyone to feel welcome.

“I am not complicit. I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn’t mean I don’t have them, and it doesn’t mean I don’t care. Nor does it mean I don’t support causes in my own, personal way.

articles.title: Night of the Coyotes review – border-crossing role-play is tourist attraction in struggling Mexican town
articles.summary: Clara Trischler’s absorbing feature sees residents of the small town of El Alberto hired to play characters in a re-enactment of the migrant experience. In contrast to other migration documentaries, which focus on the new life that awaits those who have crossed the border, Clara Trischler’s…
body: This terrifying sequence of events is later revealed to be make-believe. In the small Mexican town of El Alberto, whose population has been depleted by a steady flow of migration to the US, role-playing re-enactments function as both a means of deterrent and, oddly enough, a tourist attraction. Advertised as Caminata Nocturna – “night hike” in Spanish – these events recruit local residents to perform as specific characters, including the fearsome “coyotes”, AKA human traffickers. The attendees experience the full scale of a border-crossing operation, from being loaded on vans to intimidation from their coyotes, and police interrogation.

articles.summary: When you hire Mariska Hargitay to host the Emmys, the fact that she has a few friends in high places pays off. And that starts with Taylor Swift. “They’re genuine friends,” executive producer Dionne Harmon said.

body: The only downside is that, so delicate and subtle is his work, Whistler’s shimmering proto-modern visions are perhaps let down a little by pointing a camera at them; it’s hardly the film-maker’s fault but they just don’t jump out of the screen as they do in the gallery. articles.title: How city's market became a CBeebies TV set
articles.summary: The show, filmed in Coventry, aims to help young children explore food through their senses
body: Coventry Market's fruit and vegetable stalls, fish counters and busy walkways have become an unlikely TV set.
Cameras are rolling among shoppers and traders as local children explore unfamiliar foods for a new CBeebies series.
I Can Taste It aims to help three to six-year-olds build confidence in trying different foods through sight, smell, touch, sound and taste.
Presented by Aaron Roach Bridgeman and puppet co-host Zesty, the programme is being filmed at the market, which producers say offers children an authentic environment in which to learn about food.

articles.title: Ian Schrager Goes Public: “There’s Nothing More Boring Than a Room Full of Rich People”
articles.summary: As he prepares to open his third L.A. hotel — The PUBLIC — the Studio 54 founder and hospitality legend talks about his newly democratic door policies, getting ripped off by rivals and why he’s not afraid of failure.
body: The latest chapter is PUBLIC, built around what he calls “luxury for all,” and he is bringing it to Los Angeles inside a building freighted with somebody else’s mythology. The low-slung former motel at 8300 Sunset Blvd. was The Standard, which André Balazs opened in 1999 and ran until it closed in 2021. Balazs was Schrager’s erstwhile rival, chasing the same crowd through the boutique boom, and The Standard was his loudest answer to it: Guests checking in were treated to the view of young models in underwear lounging inside a glass fish tank behind the front desk. Until Schrager swooped in, the space had been sitting dark for five years.

He met me in the lobby in mid-August, trim and still cocky at 80, humming with the same restless energy that made him famous at 31. He is not a man resting inside his own legend. And best not to mention retirement.
“I sometimes think about doing something else,” he says. “But there’s really nothing else I like to do.”
You’re opening PUBLIC on the site of The Standard, a hotel lots of people remember very fondly. When you take over a property with that kind of history, do you try to preserve any of it?
